topics.title: Digitisation and the meaning of e-business

learn.hook: A saree weaver in Pochampally can now sell to a buyer in Toronto without leaving her village. Technology has changed not just what business sells, but how business is done.
points: Business is being digitised: activities such as buying, selling, ordering, payments, record-keeping and communication are increasingly done through computers, the internet and mobile networks.
E-business means carrying out industry, trade and commerce using computer networks. It covers all business transactions and functions conducted electronically.
E-commerce covers a firm's interactions with its customers and suppliers over the internet, i.e. mainly buying and selling online.

E-business is wider than e-commerce: besides online buying and selling, it includes internal functions such as production, inventory management, product development, accounting, finance and human resource management done electronically.

example.q: A company sells shoes on its website, and also uses an online system to track factory output and pay salaries. Which parts are e-commerce and which are e-business?
steps: Online sale of shoes to customers = e-commerce (buying and selling).
Tracking production and paying salaries online = internal functions, part of e-business.
E-business includes e-commerce plus such internal activities.
example.answer: Selling online is e-commerce; the whole set, including production tracking and payroll, is e-business.

learn.reallife: Government e-Marketplace (GeM) lets government departments buy from sellers online, and GSTN lets businesses file returns online: business and its paperwork are going digital.

topics.title: Scope of e-business: B2B, B2C, intra-B and C2C

learn.hook: When a carmaker orders tyres online, when you buy a T-shirt on an app, when HR emails your offer letter and when you sell your old cycle on a resale site, four different kinds of e-business are at work.
points: B2B (business-to-business): transactions between firms, e.g. a manufacturer ordering components from suppliers online, or dealing with distributors and dealers electronically. It helps keep inventory low and speeds up procurement.
B2C (business-to-customers): firms selling to consumers online, plus marketing, after-sales support and feedback. Customers can order any time, and firms can track preferences.
Intra-B (within business): interactions within the firm, e.g. linking departments, employees and plants through networks; it supports flexible manufacturing and coordination.
C2C (consumer-to-consumer): consumers selling to other consumers through online platforms, e.g. second-hand books, furniture or clothes; the platform provides the marketplace.

example.q: Classify: (a) a bakery chain orders flour online from a mill; (b) a student sells her old calculator to another student on a resale app; (c) a company's sales and production departments share orders on its intranet.
steps: (a) Two businesses transacting = B2B.
(b) One consumer selling to another = C2C.
(c) Within the same company = intra-B.

learn.reallife: Indian resale platforms for used cars and gadgets are C2C, online grocery apps are B2C, and B2B platforms let kirana stores restock from distributors.

learn.hook: A traditional shop needs a building, a location near customers and staff at the counter. An online shop needs a good website and a delivery partner. The differences run deep.
points: Ease of formation: e-business is easy; traditional business is relatively difficult. Physical presence: not required vs required. Location: no locational requirement vs proximity to raw materials or markets needed.
Cost of setting up and operating: low for e-business (no need for physical premises) vs high for traditional business (rent, staff, inventory).
Nature of contact with suppliers and customers: direct in e-business vs often through intermediaries in traditional business. Internal communication: non-hierarchical (direct, fast) vs hierarchical.

Response time: instantaneous vs long. Business processes are simplified in e-business. Opportunity for inter-personal touch and physical pre-sampling of products: less in e-business, more in traditional business.

Ease of global reach: more in e-business. Government support: much (e-business is promoted under IT policies). Transaction risk: high in e-business (distance and anonymity) vs low in traditional business.

example.q: A customer wants to touch and try a lehenga before buying. Which kind of business suits her, and on which basis?
steps: She wants to see and feel the product before purchase.
Physical pre-sampling is easier in a traditional store.
On the basis of 'opportunity for physical pre-sampling', traditional business scores higher.
example.answer: Traditional business, on the basis of physical pre-sampling and inter-personal touch.

learn.reallife: Many Indian brands that started online (selling eyewear, mattresses or clothes) later opened physical stores, because some customers want to try products in person.

learn.hook: A teenager in Indore can launch an online T-shirt store with a laptop and a small budget, and get her first order from Kerala the same night.
points: Ease of formation and lower investment requirements: an e-business can be set up quickly with relatively little capital, compared with a physical business.
Convenience: the internet allows business 24 × 7, so customers can shop and firms can operate at any time. This is often called 24 × 7 access.
Speed: buying, selling, information exchange and payments take place much faster; digital products like software and e-books can even be delivered instantly.
Global reach and access: an online firm can reach buyers and suppliers anywhere in the world, so the market is truly global.
Movement towards a paperless society: e-business reduces dependence on paper for orders, invoices and records, e.g. online returns, e-tickets and digital receipts.

example.q: Neeraj, a chess coach in Jaipur, starts selling recorded lessons online. Within a month he has students in Dubai and the USA and receives payments at night. Which benefits does this show?
steps: Students abroad = global reach.
Payments at night = convenience of 24 × 7 access.
Starting with just recordings and a website = ease of formation and lower investment.
example.answer: Global reach, 24 × 7 convenience, and ease of formation with low investment.

learn.reallife: E-tickets on IRCTC and DigiLocker documents are everyday examples of India's move towards a paperless society.

learn.hook: You can order a phone in ten seconds, but it may take three days to arrive, and you can't shake the seller's hand. E-business has its weak spots too.
points: Low personal touch: online dealings lack the warmth and trust of face-to-face interaction, so they suit standardised goods better than goods needing personal attention, like tailored clothes.
Incongruence between order taking and delivery speed: information and orders move instantly, but physical goods still take time to deliver.
Need for technology skills: e-business requires the ability to use IT on the part of all parties.

Increased risk due to anonymity and lack of physical presence: it is hard to verify identity and location, which can lead to fraud. People's resistance: many hesitate to adopt new technology or fear online fraud.
Ethical fallouts: e.g. firms monitoring employees' emails and online activity raise privacy concerns. Note: outsourcing (BPO/KPO) was removed from the syllabus and is not covered here.

learn.hook: From searching 'running shoes' to the doorbell ringing with your parcel, every online purchase follows the same three stages.
points: Pre-purchase/sale stage: the buyer searches for information about products and sellers; to buy, he usually registers on the website with name, address, contact details and a password, creating an account.
Ordering stage: the buyer selects items into a virtual 'shopping cart' and, once satisfied, places the order and chooses a payment method.
Delivery stage: physical goods are delivered through couriers or delivery partners; digital goods (e-books, software, music) can be delivered instantly online.

Payment mechanisms: cash on delivery (COD) (payment in cash when goods arrive); cheque (sent to the seller, goods dispatched after it clears); net banking transfer (buyer transfers money through internet banking); credit and debit cards (card details are entered and the amount is charged); digital cash (electronic money held in a bank account or wallet and used for online payment).

example.q: Arrange the steps of an online purchase: place order, register on the site, receive delivery, add items to cart.
steps: First register on the site (pre-purchase).
Then add items to the shopping cart.
Then place the order and pay.
Finally receive the delivery.
example.answer: Register → add to cart → place order → receive delivery.

learn.reallife: Cash on delivery remains popular in many Indian towns because buyers like to see the parcel before paying.

topics.title: Security and safety of e-transactions; resources needed

learn.hook: A fake shopping site, a stolen card number, a virus wiping customer records: online business is only as strong as its security.
points: Transaction risks: default on order taking or giving (seller denies receiving an order, or buyer denies placing it); default on delivery (goods not delivered, delivered late or wrong goods sent); default on payment (seller not paid, or buyer pays but does not get the goods).
Data storage and transmission risks: viruses can damage stored data; hackers may break into systems and steal or alter data while it is stored or transmitted.
Risk of threat to intellectual property and privacy: once information is online, it can be copied or misused, and personal data of customers may be exposed.

Safeguards: encryption (converting data into a code that only authorised parties can read), secure payment gateways, strong passwords and authentication such as OTPs, firewalls and antivirus software, and reliable sellers' policies.

Resources for a successful e-business: a well-developed website; technically competent staff; adequate computer hardware, software and network infrastructure; and efficient payment and delivery systems.

example.q: An online shop's customer database is stolen by someone who breaks into its server. Which risk is this, and which safeguard would have helped?
steps: Unauthorised access to stored data is hacking, a data storage and transmission risk.
Encrypting stored data and using firewalls would have protected it.
example.answer: Data storage risk (hacking); encryption and firewalls would help.

learn.reallife: Indian banks send OTPs for online card payments: a two-step authentication that makes e-transactions safer.
